title: Opening the Dhammapada
hook: 423 verses in 26 chapters, "the path of dhamma"; the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings

segments.voice: Yesterday, patipatti, camp three closed, and your line was you can do this. Is your week written down somewhere you can see it? Day one hundred fifty-seven, and camp four begins: the text.

If you've ever seen a Buddhist quote on a poster, a mug or a yoga studio wall, there's a fair chance it was claimed to come from one small book. Some of those quotes really are in it. Some are not in it at all. The real book is short enough to read in an afternoon, and deep enough to keep coming back to. For the next seventy-five days we're going to read it together, in order, a few verses at a time, so you'll know exactly what it says. Today: opening the Dhammapada.
screen: `THE QUOTE ON THE MUG.` → `SOME REAL, PLENTY NOT.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada is a collection of four hundred twenty-three short verses, arranged in twenty-six chapters. It sits in the Pali Canon, in the part called the minor collection, but its verses are anything but minor in practice. In Theravada countries it is memorized and chanted, and some people know dozens of verses by heart. The name has two halves. Dhamma you know: the teaching, and the way things truly are. Pada is a word with several meanings: a foot, a footstep, a path, and also a line of verse. So Dhammapada can mean the path of the dhamma, or the words of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma, and the tradition happily hears all of them at once. Each verse is meant to be carried: short, rhythmic, easy to remember on a walk. Each chapter gathers verses around one theme, with titles like the twin verses, earnestness, thought, flowers, the fool, the wise, anger, happiness, the elephant, and thirst. An old commentary adds a story for almost every verse, telling who the Buddha was speaking to and why, and we'll meet some of those stories along the way. We'll read it in the translation Max Müller published in 1881, in the Sacred Books of the East. His English is old-fashioned in places, and when his wording and the Pali part ways, we'll say so. Tomorrow, verse one.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `PADA — FOOT, PATH, LINE OF VERSE.` · `A STORY BEHIND ALMOST EVERY VERSE.` · `MAX MÜLLER'S ENGLISH, 1881.` · then, large: `THE PATH, IN VERSES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Here are the twenty-six chapter titles, in Müller's English. Just listen, and notice which one pulls at you. The twin verses. Earnestness. Thought. Flowers. The fool. The wise man. The venerable. The thousands. Evil. Punishment. Old age. Self. The world. The Buddha. Happiness. Pleasure. Anger. Impurity. The just. The way. Miscellaneous. The downward course. The elephant. Thirst. The mendicant. The brahmana. Which one was yours? Hold that title gently, and let the breath take over. The bell holds the time.
Dhammapada. The path of the dhamma, or the verses of the dhamma: pada means both a step and a line.
Your line: the path, in verses. Today, look up the list of chapter titles yourself and write down the one that pulled at you. We'll get there. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Dhammapada is memorized, chanted and taught, and some Buddhists know many of its verses by heart; teachers often give a talk on a single verse and the story the commentary tells about it.

original.note: Pali: dhamma (the teaching) and pada (step, path, line of verse).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Dhammapada is a book of inspirational quotes.
what it means: 423 verses in 26 themed chapters, the path of the dhamma put into lines you can carry.
what a scholar hears: it belongs to the Khuddaka Nikaya, and its commentary, the Dhammapada-atthakatha, is traditionally attributed to Buddhaghosa.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

notes: Editor review (days 151-169): cut unsourced manuscript claims (birch bark, Central Asia), 'one of the first in English' (Müller's first version was 1870) and sweeping memorization claims; replaced the manuscript myth item with one on pada.

Chapter titles are given from memory of Müller's SBE 10 table of contents (The Twin-Verses, On Earnestness, Thought, Flowers, The Fool, The Wise Man, The Venerable, The Thousands, Evil, Punishment, Old Age, Self, The World, The Buddha, Happiness, Pleasure, Anger, Impurity, The Just, The Way, Miscellaneous, The Downward Course, The Elephant, Thirst, The Bhikshu, The Brahmana); check wording, and 'mendicant' is used here for Bhikshu.
Müller's first English version appeared in 1870; the 1881 SBE edition is the one cited throughout camp four.
The Gandhari Dharmapada (Khotan birch-bark manuscript) is described as 'found in Central Asia'; confirm.
Commentary traditionally attributed to Buddhaghosa; not named here.
Practice: listening to the chapter titles, sized to a two-minute sit.
